title: Address of a Variable and Pointer Declaration
description: Write a C program that declares an integer variable `num` and initializes it with the value 10. Then, declare a pointer variable named `ptr` of type `int*` (pointer to an integer) and make it point to `num`. Print the value of `num`, its address, and the value stored in the pointer (which should be the same address as `num`).
sampleOutput:
Value of num: 10
Address of num: 0x7ffee5c01b1c
Value in ptr (address it holds): 0x7ffee5c01b1c
explanation: The output displays the value and address of num, and the address via the pointer. Output will vary if num or its address change.

title: Dereferencing a Pointer to Access Value
description: Create a C program that declares an integer variable `value` and initializes it to 25. Declare another variable, `p`, as a pointer to an integer. Assign the address of `value` to `p` and print the value of `value` using only the pointer (by dereferencing it).
constraints: You must use the pointer and dereference operator to print the value, not the variable `value` directly in the `printf` statement.
sampleOutput: The value accessed through the pointer is: 25
explanation: The output is the value set for the variable. Changing the initial value changes the output.

title: Modifying Variable Value via Pointer
description: Write a C program that declares an integer variable `data` and initializes it with a value of 50. Declare an integer pointer `dataPtr` and make it point to the `data` variable. Use the pointer to change the value of `data` to 100, then print its value before and after modification.
constraints: The modification must be done solely via the pointer, not by directly assigning to `data` again.
sampleOutput:
Original value of data: 50
Value of data after modification via pointer: 100
explanation: The output shows the value before and after pointer modification. Different initial or modified values change the output.

title: Pointer Arithmetic with Arrays
description: Declare an integer array `int arr[] = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50};`. Declare an integer pointer `ptr` and initialize it to point to the first element of this array (i.e., `ptr = arr;`). Using pointer arithmetic, print the third and fifth elements of the array.
constraints: Array size is fixed at 5. You must use pointer arithmetic, not `arr[index]` notation, to access elements after initialization.
sampleOutput:
Value of the third element using pointer arithmetic: 30
Value of the fifth element using pointer arithmetic: 50
explanation: The output shows the input array's third and fifth values. Changing the array changes the output.

title: Swapping Values using Pointers (Call by Reference)
description: Write a C program that defines a function named `swap`. This function should take two integer pointers (i.e., `int *a, int *b`) as arguments. The `swap` function's purpose is to exchange the values of the two integers. In `main`, prompt the user for two integers, call `swap`, and print their values before and after swapping.
constraints: The `swap` function must use pointers. Input integers will be between -100 and 100.
sampleOutput:
Before swap: num1 = 5, num2 = 10
After swap: num1 = 10, num2 = 5
explanation: The output shows the inputs before and after being swapped. Swapping different inputs changes the output.

title: Dynamic Memory Allocation with `malloc()` and `free()` for an Array
description: Write a C program that demonstrates dynamic memory allocation for an array of integers. Prompt the user to enter the desired `size` for the array (e.g., 5). Use `malloc()` to allocate memory for the array, read values into it, print the elements, and then free the allocated memory.
constraints: The array size `N` will be between 1 and 10. Input integers will be between -1000 and 1000.
sampleOutput:
Dynamically allocated array elements: 10 20 30
Memory freed successfully.
explanation: The output lists the input values for the dynamically allocated array. Different inputs or array sizes change the output.

title: String Reversal using Pointers (In-Place)
description: Implement a C function `void reverseString(char *str)` that takes a pointer to a null-terminated string as its argument. This function should reverse the given string in-place using only pointers (no array indexing). In `main`, read a string from the user, print it before and after reversal.
constraints: The input string will have a maximum length of 50 characters. It will consist only of lowercase English letters.
sampleOutput:
Original string: hello
Reversed string: olleh
explanation: The output shows the string before and after reversal. Different input strings will show different output.

title: Sum of Array Elements using Pointer to a Function
description: Write a C program that defines a function `int sumArray(int *arr, int size)` that takes an integer pointer (representing the beginning of an array) and an integer `size` (the number of elements). The function should return the sum of the array elements. Use this function in `main` to print the sum of a given array.
constraints: Array size up to 10. Elements will be integers between -100 and 100. The sum will fit within an `int`.
sampleOutput: The sum of array elements is: 15
explanation: The output is the sum of the values in the array. Changing the array changes the output.

title: Pointers to Pointers (Double Pointers)
description: Write a C program that demonstrates the concept of a pointer to a pointer (double pointer). Declare an integer variable `x`, a pointer to int `p`, and a pointer to pointer to int `pp`. Print the value of `x` using the double pointer, then use the double pointer to change the value of `x` and print it again.
constraints: None. The values are fixed for demonstration.
sampleOutput:
Value of x (accessed via double pointer): 10
New value of x (after modification via double pointer): 20
explanation: The output shows the value of x before and after change via double pointer. Changing initial or new values changes the output.

title: Dynamic Management of Student Names
description: Develop a C program that dynamically manages a list of student names. The program should first prompt the user for the number of students `N`. Then, for each student, it should dynamically allocate memory to store their name. After reading all names, print the list and then free all allocated memory.
constraints: Number of students `N` will be between 1 and 3. Each student name will have a maximum length of 20 characters (including null terminator). Names will consist of alphabetic characters only.
sampleOutput:
Student Names:
1. Alice
2. Bob
All memory freed successfully.
explanation: The output lists the names as entered by the user. Different inputs will change the output.
